title: How sure are we of the slope?
objectives: Compute the standard error of a coefficient.
Explain why more data and more spread in $x$ shrink it

screens.title: Ten points, one slope
screens.prose: Each point is $y = 1 + 0.5x$ plus random noise with standard deviation 1. The least squares fit to these ten points has slope 0.66, not the true 0.5.

state.caption: Dashed: the true line $y = 1 + 0.5x$. Solid: the fit to these ten points.

screens.question: We draw fresh noise at the same ten $x$ values and fit again. What slope do we get?

options.why: You kept the old noise. Fresh noise moves every point, so the fitted line moves too.
You expected the noise to cancel. With ten points it never cancels exactly, so each fit tilts a little.

options.text: A different number, usually within about 0.2 of 0.5
Anything at all, so one fit tells us nothing
options.why: You gave up on the fit. Refits are not arbitrary: they cluster round the true slope.

hints.text: The fitted slope depends on where the points land.
The noise is what pushed the slope from 0.5 to 0.66.
New noise means new points. The new slope will differ, but noise of size 1 cannot drag it far with ten points.

feedback.correct: Each fresh sample gives its own slope, scattered round 0.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changes when the noise is drawn again.

byKey.same: You kept the old noise. Fresh noise moves the points, and the fit follows them.
byKey.true: You expected the noise to cancel out. It does not cancel exactly in ten points.
byKey.any: You gave up on the fit. The refits cluster round 0.5, as the green lines show.

explain.text: Each fresh draw of noise moves the points, so each fit has its own slope. The green lines are twelve such refits. They fan round the true line, and the width of that fan is what this lesson measures.

screens.title: Noise and spread
screens.prose: The green lines are twelve fits, each to fresh noise. **Noise** sets the size of the errors. **Spread** stretches the $x$ values away from their centre, 5.5. Move both sliders and watch the fan.

derive.caption: Noise $\sigma$ = {{fixed(s, 2)}}, spread × {{fixed(w, 2)}}. Slope of the dark fit: {{fixed(0.5 + 0.16*s/w, 2)}}

screens.question: Which setting makes the fan of fitted lines narrowest?

options.why: Wide spread helps, but you left the noise high. Large errors tilt each fit more.
Low noise helps, but you bunched the $x$ values. A small wobble then tilts the line a lot.

options.text: The fan is the same width whatever we set
options.why: Move one slider at a time and watch the green lines. Each slider changes the fan.

hints.text: Move one slider at a time.
Watch the green lines near the ends of the plot.

feedback.correct: Less noise and more spread both pin the line down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set each slider to its ends in turn and compare the fans.

explain.text: Less noise puts each point nearer the true line, so each fit tilts less. Spreading the $x$ values gives the line a longer lever, so the same wobble tilts it less. Both shrink the spread of the slope.

screens.title: A thousand fits
screens.prose: We repeated the experiment 1,000 times and fitted a slope each time. The histogram counts the 1,000 slopes.

state.caption: 1,000 fits, each to fresh noise with $\sigma = 1$, at $x = 1, 2, \dots, 10$

screens.question: Which is closest to the standard deviation of these slopes?

options.why: You read the width of one bar. Almost all slopes would then sit between 0.47 and 0.53, but the bars run much wider.
You read the centre of the histogram. That is the true slope, not how far the fits spread round it.
You took the noise on one point. A slope averages ten points, so it varies far less than one point does.

hints.text: About 95% of a bell-shaped spread lies within two standard deviations of the centre.
Most of the slopes lie between about 0.28 and 0.72.
Half the width of that range is about 0.22, which is two standard deviations.

feedback.correct: About 0.11. Most slopes fall within 0.22 of 0.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the range that holds most of the slopes, then halve its half-width.

explain.text: The standard deviation of an estimate over repeated samples is its **standard error**. Here it is 0.11, so one fit usually lands within about 0.22 of the truth. Our first fit, 0.66, was about 1.5 standard errors from 0.5.

canvas.caption: Standard deviation of the 1,000 slopes: 0.11. The exact value is 0.110.

screens.title: Estimate the noise
screens.prose: In practice we never see $\sigma$. We estimate it from the residuals of our one fit. The fit chose two numbers, $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta$, so we divide the sum of squares by $n - 2$.

state.caption: Residuals of our one fit, $\hat y = -0.24 + 0.66x$

screens.question: What is $s = \sqrt{\mathrm{SSE}/(n - 2)}$ for these ten points?

hints.text: The sum of squared residuals is in the corner of the plot.
Here $n = 10$, so divide by 8.
$9.712 / 8 = 1.214$. Take the square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 9.712 by $n - 2 = 8$, then take the square root.

byKey.by-n: You divided by $n = 10$. The fit chose two numbers to hug the points, so divide by $10 - 2 = 8$.
byKey.by-n1: You divided by $n - 1 = 9$, as for a sample variance. A line spends two numbers, so divide by 8.
byKey.no-root: That is $s^2$, a variance. Take its square root to get back to the units of $y$.

explain.text: $s^2 = 9.712 / 8 = 1.214$, so $s = 1.102$. The fit picked $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta$ to make the residuals small, so dividing by 10 would understate the noise. We call $n - 2$ the residual **degrees of freedom**.

screens.title: From noise to slope
screens.prose: The explore screen showed the fan grows with noise and shrinks with spread. The exact rule, derived shortly, is $$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}}.$$ For $x = 1, \dots, 10$ the sum of squares about $\bar x = 5.5$ is 82.5.
screens.question: What is $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$ for our fit?

hints.text: Divide $s$ by the square root of the spread term.
$\sqrt{82.5} \approx 9.08$.

byKey.no-root: You divided by 82.5 itself. The rule divides by its square root, 9.083.
byKey.root-n: You divided by $\sqrt{10}$, the number of points. The slope's error depends on the spread of $x$, $\sqrt{82.5}$.
byKey.s: 1.102 is $s$, the typical miss of one point. The slope's error is that divided by $\sqrt{82.5}$.

explain.text: $\sqrt{82.5} = 9.083$, so $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = 1.102 / 9.083 = 0.121$. The simulation gave 0.110 because it used the true $\sigma = 1$. Our slope of 0.66 sits 1.3 standard errors from 0.5.

screens.title: Four times the data
screens.prose: Now each $x$ from 1 to 10 is observed four times: 40 points with the same spread. The noise estimate stays near $s = 1.102$.
screens.question: What is the new standard error of the slope?

hints.text: Each $x$ now appears four times. What happens to $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$?
The sum becomes $4 \times 82.5 = 330$.

feedback.correct: 0.061: four times the data halves the standard error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$ with every $x$ counted four times.

byKey.quarter: You divided the standard error by 4. The sum of squares grows four times, but the error shrinks by its square root, 2.
byKey.same: You kept the old sum of squares. Forty points give four times the sum, 330.
byKey.sqrt2: You doubled the sum of squares. Each $x$ appears four times, so the sum is $4 \times 82.5$.

explain.text: The sum of squares grows from 82.5 to 330, and its square root doubles. So four times the data halves the standard error, to 0.061. Precision grows like $\sqrt{n}$, not like $n$.

screens.title: No spread at all
screens.prose: A different data set: all ten readings were taken at the same value, $x = 5$.
screens.question: What is the standard error of the fitted slope?

options.text: There is none: no slope can be estimated

options.why: You read no variation as no uncertainty. The formula divides by $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = 0$, which blows up instead.
That is the standard error of the mean of $y$ at $x = 5$. It says how high the points sit, not how the line tilts.
You kept the old spread of $x$. Here every $x$ is 5, so the spread term is 0.

hints.text: Try to picture the best line through these points.
Any line through the middle of the stack fits equally well.
$\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = 0$ here. Look at what the formula does with that.

feedback.correct: Correct. With one $x$ value the slope is not identified.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which lines fit a vertical stack of points.

byKey.zero: You read no variation in $x$ as no uncertainty. It is the opposite: the slope is completely unknown.
byKey.mean: That measures the height of the points at $x = 5$. The slope needs $x$ to vary.

explain.text: Every line through the centre $(5, \bar y)$ fits these points equally well. $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = 0$, so the standard error is infinite: the slope is not identified. More readings at the same $x$ never help.

screens.title: Which divisor?
screens.prose: Four points and their least squares line. The last column holds the residuals.
screens.question: What is $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$?

hints.text: Square and add the residuals first.
SSE $= 4 \times 0.25 = 1$. How many numbers did the line estimate?
$s^2 = 1 / (4 - 2) = 0.5$. Then divide $s$ by $\sqrt 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find SSE, divide by $n - 2$, take the root, then divide by $\sqrt 5$.

byKey.n1: You divided the SSE by $n - 1 = 3$, as for a sample variance. The line estimated two numbers, so divide by $n - 2 = 2$.
byKey.n: You divided the SSE by $n = 4$. The line used two of the four points' freedom, so divide by 2.
byKey.s: 0.707 is $s$, the residual standard deviation: the typical miss of one point. The slope's error divides it by $\sqrt 5$.
byKey.sd: You took the plain standard deviation of the residuals. That is neither: divide SSE by 2, then divide $s$ by $\sqrt 5$.

explain.text: SSE $= 1$ and $s^2 = 1/(4 - 2) = 0.5$, so $s = 0.707$. Then $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = 0.707 / \sqrt 5 = 0.316$. Dividing by 3 instead would understate it by 18%.

screens.title: Where the rule comes from
screens.prose: Treat the $x_i$ as fixed and the $y_i$ as independent, each with variance $\sigma^2$, as in the model $y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \epsilon_i$, $\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$. Write $S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\hat\beta = \sum w_i y_i$ with $w_i = (x_i - \bar x)/S_{xx}$: the slope formula, since $\sum (x_i - \bar x)\bar y = 0$
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta) = \sum w_i^2\,\mathrm{Var}(y_i)$: the $y_i$ are independent and the $w_i$ are fixed
$= \sigma^2 S_{xx} / S_{xx}^2 = \sigma^2 / S_{xx}$: the squares $(x_i - \bar x)^2$ add up to $S_{xx}$
$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = s / \sqrt{S_{xx}}$: take the square root and estimate $\sigma$ by $s$

hints.text: Start by writing $\hat\beta$ as a weighted sum of the $y_i$.
Independence is what lets the variance of a sum split into a sum of variances.
Linear combination, variance of the sum, constant $\sigma^2$, add the squares, then estimate $\sigma$.

feedback.correct: $\hat\beta$ is a weighted sum of the $y_i$, so its variance is $\sigma^2 / S_{xx}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one before it: start from the weighted sum.

byKey.ind: The variance step needs $\hat\beta$ written as a sum first. Put the weighted sum above it.
byKey.se: Estimating $\sigma$ by $s$ is the last step, once the variance is $\sigma^2 / S_{xx}$.
byKey.sxx: Adding the squares needs $\sigma^2 \sum w_i^2$ first.

explain.text: $\hat\beta$ is a linear combination of independent $y_i$, so its variance is the sum of $w_i^2 \sigma^2$. Those squared weights add to $1/S_{xx}$. The derivation shows why spread in $x$ helps: $S_{xx}$ sits in the denominator.

screens.title: The intercept too
screens.prose: $$s^2 = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n - 2}, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) = s\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}.$$ The intercept is the fitted value at $x = 0$. It is less certain the farther 0 lies from $\bar x$. Our fit gives $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) = 0.753$.
screens.question: If the $x$ values are centred so that $\bar x = 0$, what is $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha)$?

options.why: You used the slope's error. With $\bar x = 0$ the second term vanishes and $1/n$ is left.
You took the error of one point. The intercept at $\bar x$ is an average of $n$ points.
You removed the noise along with $\bar x^2$. Centring removes only the $\bar x^2$ term.

hints.text: Set $\bar x = 0$ in the formula.
The term $\bar x^2 / S_{xx}$ becomes 0.
What is left is $s\sqrt{1/n}$.

feedback.correct: At $\bar x = 0$ the intercept is the mean of $y$, with error $s / \sqrt n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $\bar x = 0$ into the intercept formula.

explain.text: With $\bar x = 0$ the fitted line passes through $(0, \bar y)$, so $\hat\alpha = \bar y$. Its error is that of a mean, $s/\sqrt n$. For our data $\bar x = 5.5$, which inflates it to 0.753.

screens.title: A stock's beta
screens.prose: Sixty months of excess returns, in %: a stock against the market. The slope, the stock's **beta**, is $\hat\beta = 1.30$. The market's $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = 950$ and the fit's $\mathrm{SSE} = 3{,}480$.
screens.question: What is the standard error of $\hat\beta$?

hints.text: First find $s$ with $n - 2 = 58$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $s$ from SSE and $n - 2$, then divide by $\sqrt{950}$.

byKey.s: 7.75% is $s$, the stock's monthly idiosyncratic noise. Divide it by $\sqrt{950}$ for the error of beta.
byKey.ratio: You divided SSE by 950 without $n - 2$ or a square root. Find $s$ first.

explain.text: $s = \sqrt{60} = 7.75$% a month, and $\sqrt{950} = 30.8$, so $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = 0.25$. A beta of 1.30 sits only $0.30 / 0.25 = 1.2$ standard errors above 1. These 60 months cannot tell this stock from one that moves one for one with the market.

ideas: A fitted slope is a random variable: fresh noise gives a fresh slope. Its standard deviation over repeated samples is the standard error.
Estimate the noise by $s^2 = \mathrm{SSE}/(n - 2)$: the line spends two degrees of freedom on $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta$.
Because $\hat\beta = \sum w_i y_i$, its variance is $\sigma^2 / S_{xx}$. More data and more spread in $x$ both raise $S_{xx}$.

formula.name: Standard error of the slope
formula.note: If every $x_i$ is equal the denominator is 0: the slope is not identified.

summary.trap: $s$ is the typical miss of one point, not the slope's error. And divide SSE by $n - 2$, not $n - 1$.

quiz.prose: You can afford four times as many observations at the same $x$ values. Or you can keep $n$ and spread every $x$ twice as far from $\bar x$.
quiz.question: Which gives the smaller $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$, if $s$ stays the same?

options.why: You counted observations as the only lever. Doubling the spread also multiplies $S_{xx}$ by 4.
You may have doubled $S_{xx}$ for four times the data. It quadruples too.

options.text: They give the same standard error

options.why: Both raise $S_{xx}$, which sits under the square root in the denominator.

feedback.correct: Both multiply $S_{xx}$ by 4, so both halve the error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $S_{xx}$ under each plan.

explain.text: Four times the data adds four copies of each square, so $S_{xx}$ grows 4 times. Doubling each distance from $\bar x$ squares to 4 times each term. Either way $\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ doubles and the error halves.

quiz.prose: A fit to $n = 27$ points has $\mathrm{SSE} = 100$ and $S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = 16$.
quiz.question: What is $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide SSE by $n - 2 = 25$, take the root, then divide by $\sqrt{16}$.

byKey.s: 2 is $s$, the error of one point. Divide by $\sqrt{16} = 4$.
byKey.no-root: You divided $s$ by 16. Divide by its square root, 4.
byKey.by-n: You divided SSE by $n = 27$. The divisor is $n - 2 = 25$.

quiz.prose: From 60 months of data a stock's beta is $1.30$ with standard error $0.25$.
quiz.question: Is the stock's beta clearly above 1?

options.text: No: 1.30 is only 1.2 standard errors above 1

options.why: You compared the estimate with 1 and ignored its error. A gap of 0.30 is about one standard error.

options.text: Yes, because 0.25 is small next to 1.30
options.why: You compared the error with the estimate itself. What matters is the gap to 1, which is 0.30.

options.text: No: beta is not different from 0 either
options.why: You tested against 0. Beta is $1.30 / 0.25 = 5.2$ errors from 0, so it is clearly positive.

feedback.correct: The gap to 1 is about one standard error: well within the noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure the gap to 1 in standard errors.

explain.text: $(1.30 - 1) / 0.25 = 1.2$. A miss of 1.2 standard errors happens about a quarter of the time by chance. The data are consistent with a beta of 1.

quiz.prose: Thirty-six months of returns. The residual standard deviation is $s = 6$% a month and the market's $S_{xx} = 560$ (in %$^2$).
quiz.question: What is the standard error of the stock's beta?

byKey.root-n: You divided by $\sqrt{36}$, the number of months. The slope's error uses $\sqrt{S_{xx}}$.

explain.text: $\sqrt{560} = 23.66$, so $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = 6 / 23.66 = 0.254$. Three years of monthly data pin beta down only to about $\pm 0.5$.
